Take-Two Interactive Slides 5% as Wells Fargo Trims Estimates Behind $300 Target; Roblox Holds Flat, GameStop Barely Budges
Wells Fargo kept its bullish rating on Take-Two even as it slashed near-term estimates, and the reasoning behind that contradiction reveals just how much is riding on a single game release.
Published October 13, 2026, 1:55pm ET · 3 min read
Market Movers desk. Editor: David Moadel.
Take-Two Interactive Software (NASDAQ:TTWO | TTWO Price Prediction) stock is at $197.72, down 5% midday and off 23% year to date. Behind the drop is a Wells Fargo (NYSE:WFC) note that trimmed near-term estimates, and the selling looks company-specific because the rest of the gaming group is barely moving.
Gaming names around Take-Two tell a calmer story, and the contrast is sharp. Roblox (NYSE:RBLX) stock is flat at $49.60, holding steady even as Take-Two shares fall. Meanwhile, GameStop (NYSE:GME) stock is at $27.11, down 0.5%, a fraction of the move in Take-Two shares, and neither peer is responding to the Wells Fargo note.
The VanEck Video Gaming and eSports ETF (NASDAQ:ESPO) is flat, even though Take-Two represented 6.9% of the fund’s net assets as of June 30. For a wider benchmark, the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSEARCA:SPY) is down 0.1%, leaving Take-Two stock moving largely on its own.
Wells Fargo Cuts Near-Term Numbers but Keeps Its Overweight Call
Wells Fargo reiterated an Overweight rating and a $300 price target on Take-Two stock in the prior session. Beneath that headline, Wells Fargo trimmed its near-term bookings and adjusted EBITDA (earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization) estimates on weaker unit assumptions for the basketball franchise. Separately, Wells Fargo cut its recurrent consumer spending growth assumption on mixed player feedback to new gameplay mechanics and said Take-Two’s mobile business remains under pressure.
Looking ahead, Wells Fargo expects Take-Two’s third-quarter fiscal 2027 bookings and adjusted EBITDA guidance to come in below consensus. The rating and target remained unchanged. That is because of a Grand Theft Auto VI unit assumption that Wells Fargo places well above what it reads as implied in Take-Two’s current fiscal-year guidance. That gap is the whole debate in miniature: a weaker bridge to the release, paired with a bigger payoff once it arrives.
Gaming Group Holds Steady as Take-Two Falls Alone
Take-Two publishes the Grand Theft Auto and basketball franchises alongside a mobile portfolio, so its results turn on a few large releases and recurrent spending inside them. Roblox runs a user-generated platform, while GameStop is a specialty retailer. Each peer follows its own calendar, which keeps read-across inside this group weak.
Selling in Take-Two shares reflects a repricing ahead of a quarter Wells Fargo expects to guide below consensus, and with the VanEck fund and Roblox stock both flat, the evidence points back to the note itself.
What supports Take-Two is that the firm cutting near-term numbers kept both its rating and its target, because what it expects from Grand Theft Auto VI dwarfs the quarters in front of it. Rockstar Games, the Take-Two label behind the series, opened pre-orders in late June, and the game is scheduled to launch on November 19.
However, the bear case centers on the catalogue carrying Take-Two until that release, and both the basketball franchise and the mobile portfolio were marked down in a single Wells Fargo note, which suggests the path to launch is getting shakier. A softer bridge matters because Take-Two still reports another quarter before the release changes its results.
Take-Two’s next quarterly report lands in early November, on a date the company hasn’t confirmed, and that release is where the guidance Wells Fargo highlighted may surface. The open question is whether the pre-release catalogue holds firm enough to support the valuation until Grand Theft Auto VI ships.
The update is worth watching to see whether basketball unit trends and recurrent spending steady. Until then, TTWO shareholders may need to brace for more volatility around the report.

Take-Two shares could reach $300 as GTA VI upside remains unpriced, says Jefferies
Jefferies has reiterated its "buy" rating on Take-Two Interactive Software Inc (NASDAQ:TTWO), the video game publisher behind Grand Theft Auto, arguing that its shares could reach $300 as investors underestimate the potential of Grand Theft Auto VI.
The broker views the shares as attractive around $200, near their year-to-date lows, with a valuation of 20 times $12 in earnings per share for the year and a potential 50% upside to its price target.
Take-Two shares have fallen 17% since pre-orders opened for GTA VI, contrasting with an 18% gain during the comparable period before Red Dead Redemption 2 launched in 2018.
Jefferies argues that the market is already pricing in an outcome similar to the end of the Red Dead Redemption 2 launch cycle, despite additional growth opportunities that could distinguish GTA VI.
The broker's valuation comparison shows Take-Two trading at 20 times earnings for the second financial year ahead, below the 25 times multiple reached at a similar stage before Red Dead Redemption 2 was launched.
That valuation eventually fell to 20 times earnings by the end of 2018, when shares had retreated from their pre-launch peak and the Red Dead Online beta disappointed.
Jefferies believes the comparison understates GTA VI's potential because its online mode and a possible earlier personal computer release could generate additional sales and extend player engagement.
The broker maintains its forecast of $12 in earnings per share for the financial year 2028 and applies a 25 times earnings multiple to justifyfinancial year 2028 and applies a 25 times earnings multiple to support its $300 price target.
The potential timing of the PC version is a further reason for optimism, with GamesBeat reporting that industry sources expect it to arrive in the first quarter of calendar year 2027.
Jefferies cautions that the PC version has not been officially announced, but argues a release within months of the console launch would be significantly faster than previous Rockstar Games releases.
Red Dead Redemption 2 arrived on PC about 12 months after its console debut, while Grand Theft Auto V took roughly 19 months to make the transition.
An earlier PC release could also allow GTA VI's online mode to launch sooner, helping retain players after the initial excitement surrounding the console release begins to fade.
Jefferies sees particular potential in bringing PC players into the online environment early, including communities built around roleplaying modifications that have helped sustain the popularity of Grand Theft Auto V.
In a scenario where the PC version arrives during the fourth quarter of financial year 2027, Jefferies would cut its console sales forecast from 40 million units to 35 million.
However, the broker would add 12 million PC units, lifting projected GTA VI bookings for financial year 2027 from $2.5 billion to $2.9 billion.
The estimate includes revenue from premium editions, while Jefferies expects total bookings across the first 18 months to remain broadly unchanged or improve through an earlier contribution from the online mode.
The broker's central argument is that Take-Two's current valuation reflects a relatively cautious launch outcome, leaving investors exposed to potential upside if GTA VI's broader commercial ecosystem develops faster than expected.

Ryan Cohen keeps reaching into his own pocket to buy GameStop shares, and his conviction is pulling the entire gaming sector along for the ride. Here is what the insider buying pattern reveals about where GME could be headed.
Published September 30, 2026, 1:03pm ET · 3 min read
GameStop (NYSE:GME | GME Price Prediction) stock popped 4% to $24.79 on Wednesday, extending recent gains driven by Chairman and CEO Ryan Cohen’s continued open-market share purchases. Take-Two Interactive Software (NASDAQ:TTWO) shares advanced 3% to $209.78, while Roblox (NYSE:RBLX) stock also rose 3% to $42.53. The company recently reported a mixed quarter in which sales declined 19% while net income rose 77%, aided by cost cuts, collectibles growth, and investment gains, including from its eBay stake.
Ryan Cohen purchased 450,000 GameStop shares at approximately $23.48 each, for a total value of about $10.6 million, according to a recent SEC filing. Cohen’s direct holdings now stand near 41 million shares, representing roughly 8.8% of the company when including warrants.
These open-market buys form part of a broader pattern of insider accumulation throughout the year with no reported sales. The activity has helped sustain attention on GameStop shares even as the traditional video-game hardware and software business faces ongoing pressure.

Collectibles sales grew sharply and now account for a larger share of the mix, helped by cost discipline and non-operating gains tied to the company’s investment portfolio.
Similarities among GameStop, Take-Two Interactive, and Roblox include exposure to consumer spending on entertainment and digital content. Differences appear in business models, with GameStop emphasizing physical retail, collectibles, and balance-sheet management, while the other two focus on content creation and platform engagement. Insider conviction and a larger cash and investment position remain central to the GameStop narrative.
Ryan Cohen’s repeated purchases have provided a clear catalyst for GameStop stock in recent weeks. Strategic interest around the eBay investment and ongoing cost management continue to factor into investor discussions.

Grand Theft Auto VI Is Weeks Away. Is Take-Two Interactive (TTWO) Still a Buy at a Discount?
A video game company sitting on the most anticipated release in years would seem to deserve a premium price tag. Yet Take-Two Interactive Software (NASDAQ:TTWO) trades at a lower multiple than it has averaged over the past five years, with Grand Theft Auto VI only weeks away.
Take-Two owns Rockstar Games, the studio behind Grand Theft Auto and Red Dead Redemption, along with 2K's NBA 2K series and Zynga's mobile titles like Toon Blast and Words With Friends. It earns money when people buy its games, and even more from what they keep spending afterward on virtual currency, add-ons, and in-game items. Even with that lucrative pipeline, the video game publisher doesn't secure a spot among the 10 Best Undervalued Stocks to Buy in October. That leaves investors with a puzzle. Is the market underrating the biggest launch in the company's history, or quietly pricing in softness elsewhere in the portfolio? The answer depends on what happens after the launch-day buzz fades.
Is Cameco (CCJ) a Buy Before the Westinghouse Spin-Off?
Take-Two's real edge isn't one game. It's a catalog players keep returning to. In the fiscal first quarter of 2027, which ended in June, recurrent consumer spending made up 84% of net bookings (sales measured before accounting deferrals). That's money from people who already own the games and keep paying to play them.
The company's list of top contributors reads like a roll call of long-running franchises: NBA 2K, Grand Theft Auto, Red Dead Redemption, and mobile staples such as Toon Blast, Match Factory!, and Empires & Puzzles. Many of these are years old and still among its biggest earners. Annual sports releases run on that same repeat-spending model, which a major rival sports-game publisher depends on as well.
The fiscal first quarter wasn't a blowout. Net bookings slipped 3% to $1.39 billion, though that still landed slightly above management's guidance range. GAAP net revenue edged up to $1.53 billion from $1.50 billion, while the company posted a GAAP net loss of $34.1 million, or $0.18 per share.
The outlook is where the story lives. Management reiterated its fiscal 2027 target of $8.0 billion to $8.2 billion in net bookings, with GTA VI scheduled to arrive in November on PS5 and Xbox Series X|S. CEO Strauss Zelnick said the company expects to sustain this new level of scale and generate strong cash flows. Even with that historic growth trajectory on the horizon, the video game publisher remains noticeably absent from the 10 Best Growth Stocks to Buy Now According to Billionaires. Put that full-year target next to a $1.39 billion quarter, and it's obvious how much rides on the holiday months. CNBC reported that a recent preview of the game pointed to blockbuster demand.
What If Mobile Keeps Sliding?
The strongest objection sits in Take-Two's largest platform. Mobile net bookings fell to $739.5 million from $792.8 million, still accounting for 53% of the total. Console net revenue moved the other way, climbing to $640.5 million from $550.6 million.
That split matters. GTA VI launches on consoles, so a shrinking mobile business would leave Take-Two leaning harder on a single franchise. It's a pressure other mobile-heavy game makers have felt too. Recurrent spending dipped only 1%, so the engine underneath hasn't stalled. But mobile is the piece to watch once the launch excitement settles.
At a forward P/E of 31.05, as of October 12, investors are paying about $31 for every $1 of expected earnings. That's far below Take-Two's 5-year average P/E of 51.25, even as the company heads into the biggest product cycle in its history. It still looks pricey next to the sector P/E of 12.29. But few companies in that group are staring at a growth spike like this one. Analysts expect EPS growth of 49.70% in 2028, a pace that makes a sector-average multiple a poor fit.
There's an accounting wrinkle, too. GAAP guidance for fiscal 2027 calls for just $0.55 to $0.75 per share, so today's valuation rests on the earnings investors expect after GTA VI ships, not on this year's accounting profit. That's a bet on execution, and a big one.
Here's the tension, then. A stock that historically commanded more than 50 times earnings now sits near 31 right before its defining release. Either the market doubts the GTA VI surge will last, or it's leaving room for upside if players keep spending long after launch. That valuation gap highlights how much the market demands proven, long-tail monetization, the kind seen when Tencent Music (TME) turns streaming into a sprawling entertainment machine, rather than relying entirely on a single console release window. Hedge fund interest has risen, with 84 funds holding the stock in the most recent quarter, up from 77 in the prior one. Short interest sits at 4.45% of float, suggesting relatively limited bearish positioning.
The evidence points to a stock priced for a big launch, but not necessarily a lasting one. At roughly 31 times expected earnings, well under its own five-year norm, Take-Two looks reasonably valued if GTA VI keeps players spending for years, the way its predecessor did.
The setup suits patient investors comfortable with a hit-driven business and willing to sit through launch-quarter volatility. Would the picture change? Another delay, or mobile declines deep enough to swallow the console gains, would make even this discounted multiple harder to defend

Published October 13, 2026, 1:55pm ET · 3 min read
Market Movers desk. Editor: David Moadel.
Take-Two Interactive Software (NASDAQ:TTWO | TTWO Price Prediction) stock is at $197.72, down 5% midday and off 23% year to date. Behind the drop is a Wells Fargo (NYSE:WFC) note that trimmed near-term estimates, and the selling looks company-specific because the rest of the gaming group is barely moving.
Gaming names around Take-Two tell a calmer story, and the contrast is sharp. Roblox (NYSE:RBLX) stock is flat at $49.60, holding steady even as Take-Two shares fall. Meanwhile, GameStop (NYSE:GME) stock is at $27.11, down 0.5%, a fraction of the move in Take-Two shares, and neither peer is responding to the Wells Fargo note.
The VanEck Video Gaming and eSports ETF (NASDAQ:ESPO) is flat, even though Take-Two represented 6.9% of the fund’s net assets as of June 30. For a wider benchmark, the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSEARCA:SPY) is down 0.1%, leaving Take-Two stock moving largely on its own.
Wells Fargo Cuts Near-Term Numbers but Keeps Its Overweight Call
Wells Fargo reiterated an Overweight rating and a $300 price target on Take-Two stock in the prior session. Beneath that headline, Wells Fargo trimmed its near-term bookings and adjusted EBITDA (earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization) estimates on weaker unit assumptions for the basketball franchise. Separately, Wells Fargo cut its recurrent consumer spending growth assumption on mixed player feedback to new gameplay mechanics and said Take-Two’s mobile business remains under pressure.
Looking ahead, Wells Fargo expects Take-Two’s third-quarter fiscal 2027 bookings and adjusted EBITDA guidance to come in below consensus. The rating and target remained unchanged. That is because of a Grand Theft Auto VI unit assumption that Wells Fargo places well above what it reads as implied in Take-Two’s current fiscal-year guidance. That gap is the whole debate in miniature: a weaker bridge to the release, paired with a bigger payoff once it arrives.
Gaming Group Holds Steady as Take-Two Falls Alone
Take-Two publishes the Grand Theft Auto and basketball franchises alongside a mobile portfolio, so its results turn on a few large releases and recurrent spending inside them. Roblox runs a user-generated platform, while GameStop is a specialty retailer. Each peer follows its own calendar, which keeps read-across inside this group weak.
Selling in Take-Two shares reflects a repricing ahead of a quarter Wells Fargo expects to guide below consensus, and with the VanEck fund and Roblox stock both flat, the evidence points back to the note itself.
What supports Take-Two is that the firm cutting near-term numbers kept both its rating and its target, because what it expects from Grand Theft Auto VI dwarfs the quarters in front of it. Rockstar Games, the Take-Two label behind the series, opened pre-orders in late June, and the game is scheduled to launch on November 19.
However, the bear case centers on the catalogue carrying Take-Two until that release, and both the basketball franchise and the mobile portfolio were marked down in a single Wells Fargo note, which suggests the path to launch is getting shakier. A softer bridge matters because Take-Two still reports another quarter before the release changes its results.
Take-Two’s next quarterly report lands in early November, on a date the company hasn’t confirmed, and that release is where the guidance Wells Fargo highlighted may surface. The open question is whether the pre-release catalogue holds firm enough to support the valuation until Grand Theft Auto VI ships.
The update is worth watching to see whether basketball unit trends and recurrent spending steady. Until then, TTWO shareholders may need to brace for more volatility around the report.

Take-Two shares could reach $300 as GTA VI upside remains unpriced, says Jefferies
Jefferies has reiterated its "buy" rating on Take-Two Interactive Software Inc (NASDAQ:TTWO), the video game publisher behind Grand Theft Auto, arguing that its shares could reach $300 as investors underestimate the potential of Grand Theft Auto VI.
The broker views the shares as attractive around $200, near their year-to-date lows, with a valuation of 20 times $12 in earnings per share for the year and a potential 50% upside to its price target.
Take-Two shares have fallen 17% since pre-orders opened for GTA VI, contrasting with an 18% gain during the comparable period before Red Dead Redemption 2 launched in 2018.
Jefferies argues that the market is already pricing in an outcome similar to the end of the Red Dead Redemption 2 launch cycle, despite additional growth opportunities that could distinguish GTA VI.
The broker's valuation comparison shows Take-Two trading at 20 times earnings for the second financial year ahead, below the 25 times multiple reached at a similar stage before Red Dead Redemption 2 was launched.
That valuation eventually fell to 20 times earnings by the end of 2018, when shares had retreated from their pre-launch peak and the Red Dead Online beta disappointed.
Jefferies believes the comparison understates GTA VI's potential because its online mode and a possible earlier personal computer release could generate additional sales and extend player engagement.
The broker maintains its forecast of $12 in earnings per share for the financial year 2028 and applies a 25 times earnings multiple to justifyfinancial year 2028 and applies a 25 times earnings multiple to support its $300 price target.
The potential timing of the PC version is a further reason for optimism, with GamesBeat reporting that industry sources expect it to arrive in the first quarter of calendar year 2027.
Jefferies cautions that the PC version has not been officially announced, but argues a release within months of the console launch would be significantly faster than previous Rockstar Games releases.
Red Dead Redemption 2 arrived on PC about 12 months after its console debut, while Grand Theft Auto V took roughly 19 months to make the transition.
An earlier PC release could also allow GTA VI's online mode to launch sooner, helping retain players after the initial excitement surrounding the console release begins to fade.
Jefferies sees particular potential in bringing PC players into the online environment early, including communities built around roleplaying modifications that have helped sustain the popularity of Grand Theft Auto V.
In a scenario where the PC version arrives during the fourth quarter of financial year 2027, Jefferies would cut its console sales forecast from 40 million units to 35 million.
However, the broker would add 12 million PC units, lifting projected GTA VI bookings for financial year 2027 from $2.5 billion to $2.9 billion.
The estimate includes revenue from premium editions, while Jefferies expects total bookings across the first 18 months to remain broadly unchanged or improve through an earlier contribution from the online mode.
The broker's central argument is that Take-Two's current valuation reflects a relatively cautious launch outcome, leaving investors exposed to potential upside if GTA VI's broader commercial ecosystem develops faster than expected.

Importantly, GTA Online has also been a major positive, allowing Take-Two to generate recurring revenue through in-game purchases and additional content long after the initial sale.

Beyond the initial sales boost, the long-term opportunity also remains significant. GTA 5's continued success through GTA Online provides a strong blueprint for how Take-Two could monetize the new release for years, potentially creating a much higher recurring revenue base.

Grand Theft Auto VI Is Weeks Away. Is Take-Two Interactive (TTWO) Still a Buy at a Discount?
A video game company sitting on the most anticipated release in years would seem to deserve a premium price tag. Yet Take-Two Interactive Software (NASDAQ:TTWO) trades at a lower multiple than it has averaged over the past five years, with Grand Theft Auto VI only weeks away.
Take-Two owns Rockstar Games, the studio behind Grand Theft Auto and Red Dead Redemption, along with 2K's NBA 2K series and Zynga's mobile titles like Toon Blast and Words With Friends. It earns money when people buy its games, and even more from what they keep spending afterward on virtual currency, add-ons, and in-game items. In the fiscal first quarter of 2027, which ended in June, recurrent consumer spending made up 84% of net bookings (sales measured before accounting deferrals). That's money from people who already own the games and keep paying to play them.
The company's list of top contributors reads like a roll call of long-running franchises: NBA 2K, Grand Theft Auto, Red Dead Redemption, and mobile staples such as Toon Blast, Match Factory!, and Empires & Puzzles. Many of these are years old and still among its biggest earners. Annual sports releases run on that same repeat-spending model, which a major rival sports-game publisher depends on as well.
The fiscal first quarter wasn't a blowout. Net bookings slipped 3% to $1.39 billion, though that still landed slightly above management's guidance range. GAAP net revenue edged up to $1.53 billion from $1.50 billion, while the company posted a GAAP net loss of $34.1 million, or $0.18 per share.

CEO Strauss Zelnick said the company expects to sustain this new level of scale and generate strong cash flows. Even with that historic growth trajectory on the horizon, the video game publisher remains noticeably absent from the 10 Best Growth Stocks to Buy Now According to Billionaires. The strongest objection sits in Take-Two's largest platform. Mobile net bookings fell to $739.5 million from $792.8 million, still accounting for 53% of the total. Console net revenue moved the other way, climbing to $640.5 million from $550.6 million.
That split matters. GTA VI launches on consoles, so a shrinking mobile business would leave Take-Two leaning harder on a single franchise.
